questions.q: How has education helped women change their lives, and who pioneered girls' education in India?
answer: For a long time most girls were denied schooling because society believed a woman's place was only in the home.

answer.text: Education gives women knowledge, confidence and the ability to take up new roles — earning a living, entering professions, and taking part in public life — and so to change both their own lives and society.
In the nineteenth century, reformers such as Savitribai Phule and her husband Jyotirao Phule opened some of the first schools for girls in India, despite strong opposition.
As more girls were educated, women began to break out of old roles and to prove their abilities in every field, showing that talent is not decided by gender.

questions.q: What is the women's movement, and how does it work?
answer: The women's movement is the collective struggle of women, and those who support them, for equality and rights.

answer.text: It seeks to end discrimination and violence against women and to win them equal rights in law and in daily life.

It works by campaigning for new laws, such as those against dowry and domestic violence; by raising awareness through street plays, songs and posters; and by protesting and showing solidarity to draw attention to injustice.
The movement has secured important legal rights and greater respect for women, though much inequality still remains to be overcome.

questions.q: Why was learning denied to many people in the past, and how did some overcome this?

answer.text: In the past, education was denied to many people. Girls were often kept from school in the belief that they needed only to learn housework, and children of the poor and of so-called low castes were also kept out of learning, so that reading and writing were confined to a few.

Some brave individuals struggled against this. Reformers like Jyotirao Phule and Savitribai Phule opened schools for girls and for the oppressed castes. Learners such as Rashsundari Devi taught themselves to read and write in secret, and later wrote about their lives.
Their efforts, and the spread of schooling, gradually opened education to girls and to all sections of society.

answer: Thus learning, long denied to girls and the poor, was opened up by determined reformers and self-taught individuals.

questions.q: What are stereotypes about girls, and how can they be broken?

answer.text: A stereotype is a fixed idea about a whole group of people, applied to every member without regard to individual ability. Common stereotypes about girls are that they are weak, that they are meant only for housework, or that they cannot do subjects like mathematics and science or jobs like flying planes or joining the army.
Such ideas are false, for girls and women have shown they can excel in every field, as scientists, doctors, athletes, pilots and leaders.

Stereotypes can be broken by giving girls equal chances in education, work and sport, by encouraging them to follow their talents, and by celebrating the achievements of women who have succeeded in every walk of life.

answer: Thus false stereotypes about girls can be broken through equal opportunity, encouragement and real examples of women's success.
